title: Benchmarking quantum-annealing-based approaches for factory layout planning
authors: Xiangqian Wu, Philipp Schworm, Marcel Wagner, Jan C. Aurich
abstract: The earlystage of factory layout planning has a direct effect on the operating costs, efficiency, and productivity of manufacturing systems. Conventional automated planning approaches often face a trade-off between solution quality and computational effort. Recent studies have investigated the potential of quantum annealing (QA) for solving factory layout planning problems. However, existing studies have mainly focused on individual QA-based formulations, whereas current hybrid QA solvers support multiple model types that combine QA and classical methods. To explore the potential of QA for factory layout planning, this paper benchmarks four QA based approaches implemented with the corresponding solvers, including an iterative binary quadratic model (IBQM), a hybrid discrete quadratic model (HDQM), a hybrid constrained quadratic model (HCQM), and a hybrid nonlinear model (HNLM). To improve scalability, an iterative decomposition strategy is developed for IBQM, while a candidate selection procedure is introduced for HDQM. The approaches are benchmarked against genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization, and a hybrid tabu search and simulated annealing approach on 14 layout instances with different layout sizes, geometric complexity, spatial restrictions, and transport route configurations. The comparative analysis considers solution quality, computation time, and scalability. The results show that QA-based approaches achieve competitive solution quality and substantial computational advantages, reducing computation time by up to 94.51% relative to the classical reference methods. Among them, IBQM obtains the best solution quality in 78.6% of the instances, with a maximum improvement of 17.41% associated with an 81.34% reduction in computation time. These findings provide a basis for their further application in industrial layout planning.
summary: This paper benchmarks four quantum-annealing-based approaches for solving the complex factory layout planning problem. By comparing these QA methods against classical optimization algorithms, the authors show that QA techniques offer significant speedups and competitive solution quality. The findings establish a strong case for applying quantum computing to industrial combinatorial optimization challenges.
main_problem: The paper addresses the NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem of factory layout planning, aiming to minimize operational costs and maximize efficiency.
main_result: Quantum annealing (QA) based approaches demonstrate competitive solution quality and substantial computational advantages, reducing computation time by up to 94.51% compared to classical metaheuristics.
method: The authors benchmark four distinct QA-based formulations (IBQM, HDQM, HCQM, HNLM) against classical methods like GA, PSO, and Tabu Search.
model_or_system: The problem is formulated as an energy minimization problem encoded into a Hamiltonian, which is solved using various hybrid quantum and classical solvers (e.g., Leap Hybrid Solvers).
key_observables: Solution quality (minimum transport intensity), computation time, and scalability.
important_parameters: Layout size, geometric complexity, spatial restrictions, and transport route configurations across 14 benchmark instances.
main_assumptions: The comparison assumes that the performance gap between QA and classical methods persists across varying industrial problem characteristics.
figures_summary: Figures compare the normalized deviation from minimal transport intensity and the computation time across all tested approaches.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, reviews existing QA and classical methods, develops and refines four specific QA models, and concludes with a systematic benchmarking analysis comparing all approaches.
why_interesting: While the application is industrial optimization, the core methodology involves mapping a complex combinatorial problem onto a Hamiltonian structure suitable for quantum annealing, which is relevant to understanding quantum optimization algorithms.
